questiontext.text: In a directed graph, a strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of vertices such that:

answer.text: Every vertex can reach every other vertex in the set (both directions)

feedback.text: Correct — mutual reachability in both directions defines an SCC.

answer.text: Every vertex has the same out-degree

feedback.text: No — degree equality is irrelevant to strong connectivity.

answer.text: The vertices form a single directed path

feedback.text: No — an SCC requires mutual reachability, not just a path.

answer.text: There is at least one vertex reaching all others

feedback.text: No — every vertex must reach every other, not just one hub.

generalfeedback.text: An SCC is a maximal vertex set in which, for every pair (u, v), u reaches v and v reaches u — mutual reachability.

questiontext.text: Tarjan's SCC algorithm finds all components using:

answer.text: A single DFS that maintains low-link values and a stack

feedback.text: Correct — one DFS pass with discovery indices and low-link values.

answer.text: Two DFS passes on the same graph orientation

feedback.text: No — that resembles Kosaraju's, and its second pass uses the transpose.
No — Tarjan's uses a single DFS, not per-vertex BFS.
No — degree sorting does not identify SCCs.

generalfeedback.text: Tarjan's performs one DFS, tracking each vertex's discovery index and low-link (lowest reachable index); when low-link equals the vertex's own index, the stack top down to that vertex forms an SCC.

questiontext.text: Kosaraju's SCC algorithm runs two DFS passes. On which graph is the second pass performed?

feedback.text: Correct — the second DFS runs on the edge-reversed graph.

answer.text: On the same original graph again

feedback.text: No — the second pass uses the transpose, that is the key step.

answer.text: On the undirected version of the graph

feedback.text: No — it uses the transpose (reversed directions), not an undirected graph.

answer.text: On the minimum spanning tree of the graph

feedback.text: No — no spanning tree is involved.

generalfeedback.text: Kosaraju's: first DFS records finish times; then DFS the transposed graph in decreasing finish-time order — each resulting tree is one SCC.

questiontext.text: With adjacency lists, both Tarjan's and Kosaraju's SCC algorithms run in time:

feedback.text: Correct — linear in the size of the graph.
No — that is Warshall's transitive-closure bound, not SCC.
No — with adjacency lists SCCs are found in linear time.
No — no priority queue or sorting by weight is needed.

generalfeedback.text: Each performs a constant number of DFS passes, each O(V + E), so the total is linear O(V + E).

questiontext.text: Contracting each strongly connected component to a single vertex yields a directed acyclic graph (the condensation).

feedback.text: Correct — the condensation of SCCs is always a DAG.
Any cycle among SCCs would merge them into one, so the condensation is acyclic.

questiontext.text: Strongly connected components are defined for directed graphs.

feedback.text: Correct — SCCs are a directed-graph concept; undirected graphs use plain connected components.
SCCs require edge directions; undirected graphs have connected components instead.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Accepted — Kosaraju's is the other linear-time SCC algorithm (two DFS passes).

questiontext.text: Which statements about strongly connected components are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Tarjan's and Kosaraju's both find SCCs in O(V + E)

feedback.text: Yes — both are linear-time DFS-based algorithms.

answer.text: Contracting each SCC produces a DAG (the condensation)

feedback.text: Yes — the condensation is always acyclic.

answer.text: SCCs are defined for undirected graphs

feedback.text: No — undirected graphs use connected components; SCCs need directions.

answer.text: Kosaraju's second DFS runs on the original (un-reversed) graph

feedback.text: No — the second pass runs on the transposed (reversed) graph.

generalfeedback.text: SCCs are a directed-graph notion found in O(V + E) by Tarjan's (one DFS) or Kosaraju's (two DFS, second on the transpose); contracting them gives a DAG.
